item.title: Porcelains and Power: The Politics of Chinese Art in the Age of American Ascendancy — Wed Nov 4, 5:30 PM — Ackland Art Museum
item.description: A talk by Dr. Ian Shin (Department of American Culture, University of Michigan), co-sponsored with the Department of History. How can we understand the relationship between art collecting and Western imperialism as more than simply a story of victim and aggressor, of the plundered and the plunderer? From the Gilded Age to World War II, elite collectors and museums in the United States transformed from owning a smattering of Chinese porcelains to possessing some of the world’s largest and most sophisticated collections of Chinese art. In this talk, historian Ian Shin shows that, beyond aesthetic taste and economics, geopolitics were vital to this transformation. item.title: Reading the Image: A Workshop on Sidney Gamble's China Photographs and Papers — Thu Nov 5, 2:00 PM — Rubenstein Library Breedlove Room 349
item.description:
How do researchers move from viewing a historical photograph to understanding the people, places, and ideas behind it?
Join us for a hands-on workshop introducing archival research through the Sidney D. Gamble Photographs Collection. While thousands of Gamble's photographs documenting life in China between 1908 and 1932 have been digitized and made available online, the photographs are only one part of a much larger archival record. The collection also contains correspondence, notebooks, scrapbooks, writings, and other personal papers that illuminate how and why these images were created.
This workshop explores how archival materials provide critical context for visual sources. Participants will work with original collection materials and digitized photographs to learn how researchers connect images to personal papers, reconstruct historical contexts, and develop research questions from archival evidence.

item.title: The Journey Into Adulthood in Uncertain Times — Thu Nov 5, 3:00 PM — Sanford 223
item.description:
This presentation provides an overview of a new book, "The Journey into Adulthood in Uncertain Times," published in 2025 by Robert Crosnoe, co-authored with Shannon Cavanagh. The book tackles some key questions of interest to population scientists, developmental scientists, and the public, including: Is the lengthening span of time that young people in the U.S. take to transition into adult roles creating a new generation of "adultolescents"? How has the decades-long reshaping of this critical period of life been complicated by specific historical crises? Focusing on the United States, the answers to these questions come from integrated analyses of multiple sources of population and qualitative data. The resulting story is about gradual versus revolutionary change in the ways that young people become adults in Western affluent countries, one that grounds the growing social panic about young adults today in a more complicated but less alarming reality.

item.title: Fritz London Lecture - New frontier of Quantum Computing and Quantum Information — Thu Nov 5, 4:30 PM — None
item.description: A broad effort is currently underway to develop quantum computers that can outperform classical counterparts for certain computational, simulation or sensing tasks. The practical realization of such systems and exploration of their potential capabilities and limitations are central themes in the new field of quantum science and engineering. A central challenge in quantum computing is error suppression, which requires quantum error correction for large-scale processing. However, the overhead involved in creating error-corrected "logical" qubits-where information is redundantly encoded across multiple physical qubits-presents a significant obstacle to scalable quantum computing. In this talk, we will discuss recent advances in the programmable, coherent manipulation of quantum systems using neutral atom arrays excited into Rydberg states. item.title: “Towards an Eighteenth-Century Phenomenology of Whiteness: Madame du Barry, Zamor, and the Racial Politics of Marble” — Thu Nov 5, 4:30 PM — Smith Warehouse - Bay 10
item.description:
Alicia Caticha (Ph.D., University of Virginia) is Assistant Professor in the Department of Art History at Northwestern University. She specializes in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century European sculpture and decorative arts with a particular focus on issues of materiality, colonialism, and popular culture. Her current research takes up the racialization of the white marble ideal through the lens of its material and aesthetic relationship with the "foreign" commodities of porcelain and sugar. She has published on this topic and the decorative arts, more broadly, in Art History, Journal18, Eighteenth-Century Fiction, and The French Porcelain Society Journal. Caticha's research has been supported by the Center for the Advanced Study in the Visual Arts, the Decorative Arts Trust, and the Newberry Library. She is currently a fellow at the Alice Kaplan Institute for the Humanities.

item.title: Chamber Music Masterclass: Schumann Quartet — Thu Nov 5, 5:00 PM — East Duke 201 - Nelson Music Room
item.description:
Experience chamber music in action as students from the Duke Chamber Music Program receive coaching from the internationally acclaimed Schumann Quartet.
Formed by three brothers named Schumann and violist Veit Hertenstein, the ensemble transformed a family pastime into a celebrated international career. Praised by the Süddeutsche Zeitung for its "fire and energy," staggering virtuosity, and "willingness to astonish," the Schumann Quartet is recognized as one of today's most compelling chamber ensembles.
Through live coaching, musical exploration, and close collaboration, this masterclass offers a rare opportunity to see Duke students refine their artistry alongside four extraordinary musicians.
This event is free and open to the public. All are welcome.
Source: Duke Arts, Duke University

item.title: For The Sun After Long Nights: Covering Iran’s Women-Led Protests — Thu Nov 5, 5:00 PM — Rubenstein Library Holsti-Anderson Family Assembly Room 153
item.description:
What does it mean to report on a movement that transforms your country-and puts your own safety at risk? Join journalists Nilo Tabrizy and Fatemeh Jamalpour for a conversation about For the Sun After Long Nights, their deeply personal and rigorously reported account of Iran's Woman, Life, Freedom uprising.
Following the September 2022 death of Mahsa Jîna Amini in police custody, thousands of Iranians took to the streets in one of the country's largest uprisings in decades. Jamalpour documented the movement from inside Iran, facing the threat of arrest and imprisonment, while Tabrizy reported from abroad, knowing her coverage could prevent her from safely returning. Communicating across borders and through encrypted platforms, the two journalists forged a bond that became the foundation for their book.

item.title: Duke Arts Create: We The People: Iron Gall — Thu Nov 5, 5:30 PM — Nasher Museum of Art
item.description:
Join historian Thavolia Glymph, Peabody Family Distinguished Professor of History at Duke University and instructor of America at 250: Founding and Forging a Democracy, for a guided critical reading of the Declaration. Through discussion and analysis, participants will examine the document's language, ideas, and historical context.
Following the reading, discover how iron gall ink-used to record all important documents for a 1,400-year period of human history, including the Declaration of Independence-is made during a live demonstration. The main ingredient of this ink is made when a gall wasp lays her eggs in an oak flower, triggering the growth of a gall, rather than an acorn. This workshop will provide context from artist, Leonid Tsvetkov. To conclude the evening, participants will have the opportunity experiment with the ink and to sign their own copy of the Declaration of Independence, recreating the experience of the signers on August 2, 1776.
Source: Duke University

A miner and his sheep drift through the coal-mining landscapes of northern China. Blending observational documentary with poetic cinematic language, DRIFTING unfolds across three intertwined temporalities: geological time embedded in coal and mountains, bodily time shaped by labor and breath, and more-than-human time shared by humans, animals, and the landscape. Moving between reality and dreams, the film reflects on endurance, coexistence, and the different ways life inhabits time.

item.title: Understanding Obesity: From Stigma to Surgery — Fri Nov 6 — None
item.description:
The United States population increasingly meets the criteria for obesity. In recent years, new options for treatment have developed, and more patients are seeking support from their healthcare providers. As a result, front-line providers are tasked more frequently with assessing treatment options and managing patients with obesity. Multidisciplinary treatment requires cooperation and integration of all relevant disciplines and specialties, which are critical to provide excellent patient care, improve the patient experience, and achieve better outcomes. Understanding Obesity: From Stigma to Surgery will provide valuable information on available treatment options, including diet, psychology, medication, and surgical options. Attendees will gain an understanding of empathetic and non-judgmental approaches to patient care and will learn the impact of the interrelationship between obesity and associated health issues.
Source: Duke University

item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. item.title: Cognitive Interviewing in Survey Research — Tue Feb 2, 12:00 PM
item.description:
Cognitive interviewing in survey research is a tool that allows researchers to improve survey questions and questionnaires by better understanding how respondents understand and respond to the questions they are being asked. Data gathered through cognitive interviews help researchers identify and remedy issues with their questionnaires. This short course provides participants with fundamentals on where cognitive interviews fit in the survey process and on how to design, conduct, and analyze cognitive interviews. Participants will have the opportunity to practice specific cognitive interviewing techniques, including think-alouds, probing, and observation. Participants will also learn about revising survey questions based on interpreting cognitive interview results and about the research on which cognitive interview practices are based.

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Wed Feb 3 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

Centering the perspective of the lumpenproletariat, Notes from the Sex Worker Left asks what becomes visible when those most criminalized and excluded from respectable political life are understood as thinkers at the edge of radical political theory.
The event will feature comments by Kathi Weeks and Tania Rispoli, followed by a response from Heather Berg and open discussion.
Heather Berg is Associate Professor of Labor Studies and Gender Studies at UCLA and the author of Porn Work: Sex, Labor, and Late Capitalism. Notes from the Sex Worker Left: Lumpen Theory is forthcoming from Duke University Press in October 2026.

They’ll discuss how she assembled a 100-person, multi-university team and an industry partner in weeks, how AI and simulation are tackling “undruggable” proteins, her path toward a pulmonary fibrosis venture, and how Carolina’s innovation ecosystem moves discoveries toward patients. The event is aimed at faculty, researchers, students, entrepreneurs, industry partners and anyone curious about turning big ideas into real-world impact.

item.title: Getting Proper about Prompting: An Introduction to Prompt Engineering for Social Science and Survey Research — Fri Nov 6, 1:00 PM
item.description: Take a glance through recent news or social media and you would be hard-pressed not to see mentions of chatbots and artificial intelligence (AI) methods aimed at generating text, images and other content. Recent work by Eloundou and colleagues (2023) explored the potential impact of these types of generative AI on labor markets, and survey research, specifically was among the top two most impacted industries. Professor Andrew Ng has been cited as saying “AI won’t replace human workers, but ‘people that use it will replace people that don’t.’” Much of the way researchers in the social sciences and survey research are incorporating AI into their workflow involves some type of prompting. Prompt Engineering approaches along with more nuanced fine tuning approaches are being used and refined to better incorporate more robust approaches for AI incorporation into the research process.
